key: A portion of Mine own Self, transformed in the world of life into an immortal Spirit, draweth round itself the senses of which the mind is the sixth, veiled in matter.
s: Having named his supreme abode, from which none return, Krishna turns to the embodied soul; Śaṅkara (Advaita), Gītā Bhāṣya 15.7, reads this portion as a portion only in imagination, like the sun reflected in water, which returns to the sun once the water is removed.
src: Śaṅkara, Gītā Bhāṣya 15.7, trans. A. Mahadeva Sastri, 2nd ed. (1901), archive.org bhagavadgitwith00agoog

opened.edition: A. Mahadeva Sastri, The Bhagavad-Gita with the Commentary of Sri Sankaracharya, 2nd ed. (1901) (OCR)
opened.locator: chapter 15, commentary on 15.7 (read with 15.1 to 15.20, esp. the question closing 15.6)

evidence.words: He is like the sun reflected in water ; the reflected sun is but a portion of the real sun ; and on the removal of water the reflected sun returns to the original sun and remains as that very sun. … Our theory is not open to this objection ; for, it is only a portion limited by the up^dhi sjet. up by avidy^ ; it is a portion as it were, an imaginary portion.
evidence.lang: English (Mahadeva Sastri’s 1901 translation of the Sanskrit)
evidence.gloss: The individual soul is like the sun reflected in water: the reflection is only a portion of the real sun, and when the water is removed it returns to the original sun and remains that very sun. [To the objection that the partless Supreme Self can have no portion:] it is only a portion limited by the upadhi set up by avidya, a portion as it were, an imaginary portion.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 15.7, at 556); Telang 15.7 (an eternal portion of me) confirms the sentence builds on no Besant-only word. Plain sense faithful: 15.6 closes on the supreme abode whence none return and 15.7 to 15.11 turn to the soul in the body; no four-word run from the verse. In the packet, Sankara closes 15.6 by asking how those who reach the abode do not return, and answers at 15.7 with the sun reflected in water returning to the original sun when the water is removed, then, to the objection that the partless Self has no parts, calls the portion one limited by the upadhi of avidya, a portion as it were, an imaginary portion. The sentence paraphrases both without drift. Evidence pieces re-found by squash match against the packet. entry-check ok.
